name: Trouser turn-ups (cuffs)

card.summary: Trouser turn-ups (cuffs) are folded-up hems that add visual weight at the ankle, helping the trouser hang straight and giving the leg line a finished, structured look.

quick.overview:
A turn-up (called a cuff in American English) is made by rolling the bottom of the trouser leg outward and sometimes pressing or stitching it into place. It is a tailoring detail that finishes the hem.

Style-minded dressers use cuffs to add a little weight to the hem so the trouser falls cleanly, and to adjust where the leg ends relative to the shoe. Whether they suit a person depends on build, leg length and trouser cut.
quick.how: Cuffs are specified at the tailor or sewn into ready-made trousers, often with a width of a few centimetres. They are most common on tailored and chino-style trousers, and are paired with ankle-length or shoe-skimming lengths.
quick.risks: There are no health risks. Style commentators note that cuffs interrupt the line of the leg and may not flatter everyone, particularly very short trousers or very slim fits; preferences vary.

lead: Trouser turn-ups, known as cuffs in American English, are formed by rolling the finished hem of a trouser leg outward, and are sometimes pressed or stitched in place.[1] Hemming itself prevents the edge from fraying; the fold adds a band of fabric at the ankle.[1]

In personal style, people use cuffs to give trousers a more structured finish. The extra fabric adds a little weight to the hem so the leg drops straight, and the horizontal band can shorten the visual length of the leg slightly, which wearers adjust through the cuff depth and trouser length.

angle.text: A cuff adds weight and a defined edge at the hem, so the trouser falls straight and the length can be tuned to the shoe. Wearers use it as a tailoring detail to polish the outfit.

infobox: Hem rolled outward, pressed or stitched

paras: A cuff is made by folding the bottom of the leg outward after hemming, then pressing or stitching the fold so it holds.[1] The same effect can be created by rolling casual trousers or jeans without tailoring.

People choose cuffs for the visual weight at the hem and to control where the trouser ends relative to the shoe or ankle. Cuffed and uncuffed styles are both common, and tailors offer cuff widths according to taste and body proportions.
